review:
Dark Quest 2 is a turn-based dungeon crawler that openly embraces the spirit of classic tabletop fantasy adventures while presenting them through a charming board game-inspired format. Developed and published by Brain Seal Ltd, the game acts as both a tribute to old-school strategy RPGs and a streamlined dungeon-crawling experience focused on tactical combat, exploration, and party management. Rather than attempting to modernize the genre with overwhelming complexity or cinematic presentation, Dark Quest 2 builds its identity around simplicity, nostalgia, and strategic encounters that feel heavily inspired by traditional pen-and-paper campaigns.

The game immediately establishes its tabletop influence through its presentation. Characters move across environments that resemble handcrafted board game maps filled with miniature-style figures, dice-inspired mechanics, traps, treasure chests, and dungeon layouts that feel physically assembled rather than digitally generated. This visual direction gives the adventure a unique personality that separates it from more conventional fantasy RPGs. The entire experience feels like participating in a living tabletop campaign guided by an unseen dungeon master, complete with narrated introductions and fantasy storytelling framed through a playful board game aesthetic.

The story itself is intentionally straightforward. Players assemble a party of heroes and guide them through dangerous dungeons while battling monsters, avoiding traps, and attempting to defeat an evil sorcerer threatening the realm. Narrative depth is not the game’s primary focus, but the lighthearted fantasy atmosphere works well because the experience is more concerned with recreating the feeling of a tabletop adventure than delivering an emotionally complex storyline. The simple structure keeps pacing efficient and allows players to focus on dungeon exploration and tactical decision-making.

Combat forms the core of the experience, and it succeeds largely because of its accessibility and strategic pacing. Battles unfold on grid-based maps where positioning, movement range, attack timing, and environmental awareness become critical. Unlike faster action RPGs, Dark Quest 2 rewards patience and careful planning. Every move matters because enemies can quickly overwhelm careless players through numbers, traps, or coordinated attacks. The turn-based structure creates a satisfying tactical rhythm where players must constantly evaluate risk versus reward before committing to actions.

Each playable hero contributes unique strengths and abilities to the party. Warriors absorb damage and dominate close combat, wizards unleash devastating magical attacks, and archers or rogues provide ranged support and utility. Managing the balance between these different classes becomes one of the game’s most rewarding aspects because success often depends on using each hero efficiently rather than relying on brute force alone. Positioning weaker characters behind stronger front-line fighters while controlling enemy movement creates encounters that feel surprisingly tactical despite the game’s relatively straightforward mechanics.

Progression systems add another layer of satisfaction. Heroes gain access to stronger equipment, improved abilities, and better combat options as the campaign advances. Discovering magical items and upgrading party members provides a steady sense of improvement that keeps dungeon exploration rewarding. The game also introduces environmental hazards, traps, and puzzle-like scenarios that force players to think carefully about movement instead of simply attacking enemies directly. Certain encounters feel almost like miniature strategy puzzles where efficient positioning and timing become more important than raw power.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is its pacing. Levels are generally compact enough to avoid becoming exhausting, and combat encounters rarely overstay their welcome. This structure makes Dark Quest 2 especially enjoyable in shorter play sessions because meaningful progress can usually be made without committing to extremely long dungeon runs. The campaign steadily introduces new enemy types and mechanics, helping maintain variety as players progress deeper into increasingly dangerous environments.

Visually, the game’s board game presentation remains consistently charming throughout the adventure. The miniature-inspired character models, handcrafted environments, and animated dice-roll style effects give the game a personality that feels both nostalgic and inviting. Rather than aiming for realism, Dark Quest 2 focuses on creating the illusion of a fantasy tabletop session brought to life digitally. The colorful environments and exaggerated designs reinforce the game’s lighter tone while still maintaining a sense of adventure and danger.

The soundtrack and narration also contribute heavily to the atmosphere. Fantasy-inspired music accompanies exploration and combat without becoming overly dramatic, while the narrator adds personality to dungeon introductions and story sequences. This narration further reinforces the tabletop campaign feeling, making the player feel as though a dungeon master is guiding the adventure from behind the scenes.

The game’s simplicity, however, can also become one of its biggest weaknesses. While the accessible mechanics make it approachable for newcomers, players looking for deeper tactical systems may eventually find combat somewhat repetitive. Enemy AI is functional but not especially sophisticated, and encounters often rely more on numerical pressure than highly advanced strategy. Compared to larger tactical RPGs with complex class systems and extensive customization, Dark Quest 2 remains relatively lightweight in scope.

The campaign also lacks strong narrative depth. Characters are functional archetypes rather than deeply developed personalities, and the story rarely evolves beyond traditional fantasy adventure themes. Players expecting emotionally driven storytelling or elaborate worldbuilding may find the narrative too basic to remain memorable outside the gameplay itself.

Another limitation is the repetition inherent in the dungeon structure. While the game introduces enough variety to remain entertaining for most of its runtime, some later encounters begin to feel mechanically familiar. The relatively simple progression systems and straightforward objectives occasionally make longer sessions feel repetitive, especially for players accustomed to more elaborate strategy RPGs.

Despite these shortcomings, Dark Quest 2 succeeds because it understands exactly what kind of experience it wants to provide. The game does not attempt to become an overwhelmingly deep tactical simulator or a cinematic role-playing epic. Instead, it focuses on recreating the fun of a classic tabletop dungeon crawl through accessible combat, charming presentation, and satisfying party progression. Its straightforward design philosophy gives it a relaxing quality rarely found in more complicated strategy RPGs.

Dark Quest 2 ultimately feels like a digital board game designed for players who enjoy old-school fantasy adventures, tactical combat, and tabletop-inspired dungeon crawling. While it may not possess the depth or scale of larger RPG franchises, its charming visual style, accessible mechanics, and consistently enjoyable combat make it an entertaining and highly approachable strategy experience.

This is my substitute for Hero Quest

Being a huge enthusiast of board game dungeon crawlers like Talisman, HeroQuest and such I tried looking for similar games on Steam and came up with the Dark Quest series. Given it was already on sale, I decided to give Dark Quest 2 a go.

It's a nice little HeroQuest clone that is pretty much exactly what I was looking for. You start out with a single hero and then on subsequent runs you recruit other characters to come with you to complete a campaign comprising of a couple dozen maps until you eventually get to the end. Each map is a small dungeon maze with rooms and corridors and everything is turn based including movement just like a board game. There aren't too many stats to worry about, nor any of the more advanced systems of modern RPGs. Everything here is kept as simple as possible, in the spirit of board games of the olden age. 

This is a game which evokes memories of simpler times, doesn't take hours to play and is very easy to master. The gameplay boils down to clearing a dungeon, defeating the enemies and grabbing all the loot you can find. There is a moderate difficulty to each dungeon, but you may grind them as many times as you want by replaying the same map over and over with a slight incline in enemy difficulty on each subsequent pass. However, ballancing out your party lets you explore new possibilities and cover the skills required to beat each level. Following each level, you go back to town, where you can buy better equipment, acquire new skills and get some other bonuses to help out.

There are many maps in the campaign with many more available in the Steam Workshop if you're up for a challenge. It will take a little while to get through all of the maps to reach the end because of the slow nature of the game. That being said, the game brings back nostalgic memories of playing D&D board games from my childhood and as such is a great way to burn some time with when one wishes to unwind after a long day. 

I'm pretty sure I'll be spending more time with this title and recommend it to anyone who's into fantasy themed tactical gameplay and/or looking for an equivalent to playing a board game dungeon crawler on their PC.

Gráficamente está bien sin ser una maravilla, pero da aspecto de pintado y queda bastante resultón. El control como tal, no existe, pero si que tiene defectos en el manejo o ausencias (luego lo comento). La música está bien, acompaña, pero poco más.

Es como una especie de juego de mesa, tenemos misiones y un poblado para reponer fuerzas, comprar y vender objetos, armas, etc. y mejorar a nuestros héroes. Tiene bastante variedad de habilidades y personajes, lo que da para jugar de diferentes formas y combinaciones, todas funcionales (esto es muy importante). Hay habilidades pasivas y activas, debemos elegir sabiamente.

Las partes negativas, el control, a pesar de ser con el ratón y no requerir gran cosa, a veces es un poco torpe, puedes sin querer hacer alguna acción que no era lo que querías. Le falta también el poder rotar el mapa, ya que a veces quedan cosas un poco fuera de la vista, y en los menús, tanto del poblado como durante el juego, también creo que es bastante mejorable.
Otra cosa negativa, es que tiene solo un mundo, hubiera estado bien al menos dos y tres ya perfecto.

Recomendado para cualquier amante de los juegos de mesa tipo rol simple. No esperes un Baldurs Gate 3. Y como ya he comentado, si te gusta y te pica, acabas jugando bastantes horas, primero para conseguir partida e ir mejorando, y luego para probar diferentes combinaciones de personajes.

Fun game, and a lot of improvements and additions over DQ1.  That said...

The combat is not designed so that you can escape without damage, from most encounters (without extreme luck).  As such, potions (healing potions) are basically required to succeed at a lot of quests, and you can't heal outside of a quest without paying money to rest your party at an inn, or taking along the cleric, who.. doesn't heal very much.  If you get a full party wipe, you can resurrect cheaply (also costs gold, however), but you don't get to recover consumables, which basically puts you in a real bad spot if you wipe -- you need to have some serious gold in the bank, to recover, despite the low resurrection fee.  To recover, you need to partially do quests, and abandon them, to reclaim a small amount of gold until you can get enough to both heal damage, and buy more potions.  This is the epitome of boring grinding, to recover from just a failure or two.

Hesitant thumbs-up.  Certainly better if you can appreciate the Ironman-esque nature of the game.

Tip: Think about character healing abilities, early on, to save some gold costs... or play easy mode, which effectively heals you some at the end of each quest.

Ech, you got me, I'm a total sucker for isometric perspective, classic RPG themes and turn-based combat. Bought this game quite a while ago, but never checked it out, as there were always more interesting alternatives to play. But the time has finally come, and I gave it a try.

Surprisingly, this is actually a quite decent casual little game. Don't expect a lot of strategic depth or polished RPG system - it's something meant to be played on tablets - but it's fun enough to click around for a while if you happen to be laying bedridden.

Painted graphics are really nice, dungeon locations look cute, the gameplay is simple, but engaging enough to spend about 8 hours completing the main campaign. Six not exactly balanced character classes to choose from to form your 3-man party, there are also very simple skill progression and item systems. Default difficulty offers a bit of a challenge and the the whole adventure will most likely be over before it will get boring. Game has a map editor, so there's some more replayability in the form of downloading user created maps through steam workshop. I actually played the whole thing twice back to back with different party setups.

If I wanted to nitpick, UI is not exactly stellar, often characters are blocking with their sprites certain tiles you'd like to move to. I'd also wish the game was somewhat longer, but I guess the price is fair for what the game has to offer. 

As long as your expectations are not too high, you should have some fun with this title.

The game seemed like simple fun at first glance and I thought I could get into, unfortunately it was very poorly made. 
For starters the technical issues were plenty. I’ve had mission-ending bugs, I’ve had clipping issues, I’ve had tooltips remain on screen even though I closed the window. The QoL wasn’t any good either, there are no keyboard shortcuts or key bindings, there isn’t any option to rotate the camera, you cant leave mid mission and the worst of all whoever made that menu should consider hitting himself in the head a few times, who the hell puts exit game right under the options as a huge button? ended 3 runs early thanks to that poor design, at least there is a game speed increase, it would’ve been absolutely unplayable if lightspeed wasn’t an option. 
And there are other random things that are simply annoying, like one particular character having a resurrect spell where you target the remains of your allies to do so, and another class having an ability that makes clones of itself, very normal things you would think but oh no, if a clone dies it leaves behind remains as well, and believe me resurrecting a clone instead of the main hero is annoying as hell, WHY WOULD YOU EVEN HAVE THAT in the game!!???
This game could have potential but as it is its just a joke, a student project at best.

Ultimately, what should be a good game is let down by mechanics and the type of difficulty. It just gets very boring and very samey and very grindy in a very short while. This could have been a great game, but sadly it isn't. 

UI Issues:

Drag and drop of portraits is finicky and its possible to glitch the portraits so you have 2 of 1 hero. if you don't place it within the small hidden inner drop zone then it doesn't register.

You can't see what is on the ground when an enemy or object is in the foreground. Since you need to target a location or object to move or cast a spell, you will need to jog your party around to click on exit locations and forget casting resurrection in combat if there is an enemy in the foreground hiding the body of your fallen hero.

AI is simplistic, so to cover this the game has preset levels, and since you only get one use of each ability (in general) per quest, knowing when to use each ability is basically a case of having played the level before. 

RNG: enough said. 

Most of the craftable items have absolutely no value. There is always a "best" item, because of the way enemies work.

Late game enemies deal unblockable chaos damage. Have fun wading through a room full of ranged unblockable damage while your heros are being spam-feared 

In the end I didn't finish it. The story is boring. The levels are insipid,. the characters are mostly lackluster and the few redeeming elements are swallowed up by the mess of the rest. After recovering 2 pieces of the amulet, and needing to get the third, I literally felt a sense of dread of having to play another quest. That's when I stopped. 

I'll add that the game marketing is extremely misleading.

The "Skull of Fate"? That just means your character avoids death once per Fate level you have, and survives with 0 hp (so 1 more hit will kill them). The game also has enemies that have Fate, mostly undead. There's no "twisted fate" to discover, this is simply a "if you take damage that would kill you, instead reduce hp to 0, consume 1 fate".

Likewise the "discover hidden doors". There's no hidden doors, they all are clearly visible and actually required to go through to complete the quest in most cases. They all also have exactly the same form of a raised tile which the game introduces you to in the very first quest. 

Pick it up if it's on high discount, and you just want to waste an hour or two tooling about, but big miss otherwise.
